name: Harold Holt
bio: One of the young men of George Ives's household; Cook identifies him as Ives's grandmother's former secretary, named alongside James Goddard as sharing Ives's rooms at E4 the Albany - and sometimes his bed - from 1894.
bio_sources: Cook, London and the Culture of Homosexuality (2003), pp. 146, 148
bio_note: Cook 2003 p. 146 (read in the source) names the two men sharing Ives's bed as 'James Goddard (Kit)' and 'Harold Holt (Cubby)'. Cook 2014 p. 101 (PDF 112, folio confirmed, read in the source) instead identifies the long-term resident nicknamed Cubby as 'Charles Gee'. Facts from Cook, London and the Culture of Homosexuality (2003), p. 146 (PDF 162; printed folio confirmed). Dates: not found; recorded as unrecovered, and note that the source position is weaker for him than for the rest of the household. Harold Holt does not appear in Cook 2014 at all - a search of the whole PDF returns no occurrence of the name - so the only source for him remains Cook 2003 p. 146, which names him but gives no dates, and Cook 2014 assigns the nickname Cubby to a different man (Charles Gee), the unresolved conflict already recorded above. Searched so far, without result: Cook, Queer Domesticities (2014), PDF - every occurrence of the surname in the whole book, plus the endnotes and bibliography for the household chapter; the Ives repo transcripts (ives_diaries_burnet.txt, ives_letters_burnet_collated.txt, ives_letters_burnet_transcription.txt, ives_lewis_correspondence_2026-06.md), which contain no occurrence of any of the household surnames; and the open web, which returned only the Palgrave chapter version of Cook's same text ('George Ives, Queer Lives and the Family') and no dates. Cook is the only scholar to have written this household up and he dates their arrivals, their departures and Ives's will, but never a person: he gives no birth or death date for any member of the household. Unresolved without census, GRO index and probate research on common English surnames. Ives's own proved will (Cook, printed pp. 109-110), which leaves the Adelaide Road house to Bloodworth and Saunders, names Bloodworth an executor and portions the Goddards, is the natural documentary starting point, since a grant of probate fixes addresses and often identifies legatees.
